personas.name: Maria
personas.title: Front desk clerk
personas.description: Runs the front desk: takes bookings, and checks guests in and out.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To tell a guest at once whether a room is free for their dates, and hold it
  for them, without ever giving the same room to two guests.
- To check guests in and out quickly, so nobody waits at the desk.
- To know which rooms are ready before a guest arrives, without phoning
  housekeeping.

## Knows

Every room in the hotel, the regulars, and the cancellation policy by heart.
Comfortable with a computer, but has learned the system on the job, not from a
manual.

## Context

At the desk all shift, on a shared desktop, with a guest or the phone waiting
most of the time. Interrupted constantly, so anything they start may be finished
minutes later.

## Expects

The paper diary's view of the hotel: rooms down the side, nights across the top.
Talks about stays, rooms and arrivals, not reservations or inventory.

## Cares about

Never having to tell a guest standing in front of them that their room was given
away. They'll go back to the paper diary the first time the app gets that wrong.

personas.name: Ana
personas.title: Housekeeper
personas.description: Cleans and readies the rooms between guests.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To know which rooms to clean first, so arriving guests don't wait for a room.
- To tell the front desk a room is ready without walking back down to say so.

## Knows

The building, floor by floor, and how long each kind of room takes. Uses a phone
every day, but rarely for work.

## Context

On their feet, moving from room to room with a trolley, a phone in their pocket.
Gloves on much of the time, so anything they do has to take a tap or two.

## Expects

A list of rooms, in the order they'll do them. Talks about rooms being clean,
dirty or ready.

## Cares about

Not being rushed by the front desk for a room they didn't know was urgent.

personas.name: David
personas.title: Hotel manager
personas.description: Runs the hotel, and answers for its takings to the owners.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To set what each room costs, night by night, so busy dates earn more.

## Knows

The local market and the hotel's busy seasons. Reads a spreadsheet well, and
expects software to do the arithmetic for them.

## Context

At a desk in the back office, a few times a week, in between everything else
running a hotel brings.

## Expects

A calendar of rates, like the one they keep in a spreadsheet today.

## Cares about

Rates they can change in a minute when a big event is announced, and being sure
the front desk is quoting them.

tradeoffs.name: One room per booking
tradeoffs.description: A booking holds one room, not several.
tradeoffs.benefit: Booking, changing and cancelling stay simple: each booking is one room for one stay.
tradeoffs.drawback: A family that needs two rooms makes two bookings. Group bookings is where several rooms under one name is being explored.

tradeoffs.name: Front desk bookings only
tradeoffs.description: Bookings are taken at the front desk, not from online travel agencies.
tradeoffs.benefit: No agency integrations to build or keep working, while most bookings come straight to the desk.
tradeoffs.drawback: Clerks enter each agency booking by hand, as it arrives by email.

tradeoffs.name: Migrations run while the old release serves
tradeoffs.description: Migrations run before the new image starts, while the old one is still serving, rather than stopping the app for each release.
tradeoffs.benefit: Releases don't take the front desk offline.
tradeoffs.drawback: The running code has to work with the new schema for a minute, so a column is added a release before it's used, and removed a release after the code stops reading it.

tradeoffs.name: Database constraint, not an app lock
tradeoffs.description: The database refuses overlapping bookings with an exclusion constraint, rather than the app locking the room while it checks.
tradeoffs.benefit: No two bookings can overlap, however they arrive at once, without the app having to get locking right. The check in the app is only there to give clerks a clear message first.
tradeoffs.drawback: Bookings need Postgres with `btree_gist`, so they can't move to a database without it.

Offline sync with conflict resolution, background sync, and retry queues, unless syncing is the question.
A delivery queue, dead-letter handling, or delivery guarantees, when sending once is enough to see it work.

implementation.text: Real storage, with data that may be reset, and those using it told before a reset when it holds their real work.
A managed database's default backups left on when it holds real work, since they cost nothing to keep.
A simple forward migration, rather than a reset, when people still act on the records.
A script to reset or seed its data.
Before a build changes how data is stored on the device, work not yet sent is sent or carried over, and data it can't read is set aside, not deleted.
Output it can rebuild by running again from the source, so a reset loses nothing, and a time limit on each run so one that hangs shows as failed.
Files it writes into people's repos never overwrite their edits without asking.

overengineering.text: Down migrations, restore drills, rollback plans.
Failing over to a second provider.
Dead-letter queues and retry policies, when a failed message can be seen in the logs and resent by hand.
Background sync, resumable uploads, and retry schedules, where syncing when it opens works for those trying it.
Repair tools or automatic backups for data kept on the device.

levels.summary: Enough that people's data is safe and a bad release can be undone.

outcomes.text: Data that people or systems put in is kept across changes.

implementation.text: Versioned migrations run by the release, never by hand.
A down migration, or a backup taken before a risky change.
Automated backups, such as a managed database's defaults, even before a restore has been tested.
Queued and scheduled work, such as tomorrow's reminders, kept across deploys and restarts.
Output that can be rebuilt from its source counts as kept while the source still has it. History only it holds is backed up.
Local data migrated on upgrade, from a copy taken first and kept until the new version has opened it.
Work captured on the device kept where the OS won't clear it until the server confirms it has it, and safe to send again.
Where its local data is kept documented, so people's own backups include it.
Config files people wrote for it, and files it wrote, still work after an upgrade.

overengineering.text: Restore drills.
Snapshots of every run's output kept just in case.
A cloud backup or sync service for data on devices, when people's own backups cover where it's kept.
Versioned config schemas with automatic migration, when older config simply keeps loading.

outcomes.text: A bad release can be undone.

implementation.text: A rollback to the previous release.
Migrations that add before they remove, so the previous release still runs after a rollback.
It can be switched off quickly without a release, such as with a kill switch.
A quick fixed release.
A fixed release can open data the bad release already wrote or migrated.
The previous version made the default install again, such as by moving npm's latest tag back or reverting the Homebrew formula, and the bad one deprecated.
A remote switch and a minimum-version check in the first build people rely on, since builds already out can't gain them later.
A phased or staged rollout that can be paused if crash reports climb.
Processing paused without a release, with queued work held until it resumes, and output a bad release wrote rebuilt by rerunning those runs.

overengineering.text: A remote kill switch, and a service to host it, for installed software with no backend.
Automatic rollback to the previous version on people's devices.
Over-the-air code updates to get around store review.

outcomes.text: When something it depends on is slow or down, it fails clearly or degrades gracefully instead of hanging.

implementation.text: Timeouts on every call to a dependency, with retries only where they're safe.
A message or call that can't go through retried later or marked failed where someone will see it, never dropped.
Messages to others' systems, such as webhooks, retried with backoff when the receiver is down, and given up on after a set time with the failure recorded.
A run that can't finish leaves the last complete output in place, or marks its own as incomplete.
A clear message and a non-zero exit when a service it calls is down or too slow, so a CI job fails instead of hanging.
An unreachable update server or service never blocks the work people can do without it.

overengineering.text: Chaos testing, or running in several regions.
A transactional outbox or worker service for webhooks, when sending after the write and logging failures is enough.
A second provider to fail over to, before the first one's outages are shown to matter.
A message broker or separate queue service, when a table in its own database is enough.
Timeouts, retries, or fallbacks inside a library that calls nothing, or whose caller already retries.
Making screens work offline that aren't used offline.

levels.summary: Enough to depend on: it rides out failures, and recovery is proven.

outcomes.text: It holds up under overlapping runs, partial failures, and retries.

implementation.text: Operations safe to repeat, such as with idempotency keys or upserts.
Tests for two runs at once, and for retrying after a crash halfway through.
It fails safe where failing could cause harm, stopping rather than charging twice, sending twice, or acting on bad data.
A write that takes several steps done in one transaction, so a crash halfway leaves nothing half saved.
Rerunning any time range rebuilds what it produced, a run that starts while another is going waits or exits, and it stops when the source's data no longer has the shape it expects.
Deliveries to endpoints others run retried for a set time, then set aside for replay, so one receiver's outage doesn't hold up the rest.
Sync picks up where it left off after the app is killed or the connection drops, with IDs made on the device so a retry isn't new work.
Cancelling it, or the CI job running it, leaves nothing half-done, or a rerun finishes the job.

overengineering.text: Exactly-once delivery, where safe retries and duplicate checks are enough.
A workflow orchestrator or distributed lock service for one job on one schedule, where the scheduler's no-overlap setting or a database lock is enough.
Retries, locking, or idempotency handling in pure functions that do no I/O.
A general-purpose sync engine or CRDTs, where one person owns each record and a simple rule settles conflicts.

outcomes.text: It meets its availability target.

implementation.text: An agreed availability target, such as 99.9%, that's measured.
Its data ready by an agreed time, and queued work handled within an agreed time.
A target that fits when it's used, such as the hours its users work, and that allows for what it depends on.
Usually not applicable on people's own devices: what matters is that its main work keeps going when the services it calls are down.
Usually not applicable: the software using it holds the target.

overengineering.text: Running in several regions, or failover, beyond what the agreed target needs.
A round-the-clock target, or more nines, for work used only in business hours.
A target higher than what it depends on can deliver.
An availability target for software that runs on people's own devices.
Offline support for parts its users only use when connected.

outcomes.text: Recovering from a bad release or a loss of data is known to work.

implementation.text: A rollback that's been practiced, including upgrading, downgrading, and upgrading again.
A staged rollout that can be paused, and a minimum supported version raised with notice, after work not yet sent has finished sending.
A bad version deprecated and the previous one made the default again, tried once before it's needed.
Automated backups, with a restore that's been tested.
How much data a loss could cost, and how long recovery may take, agreed and shown in a restore test.
Output it can rebuild restored by rerunning from the source, with how far back the source keeps data known.
A copy of the local data taken before each migration, with a tested way to put it back.
For data kept only on people's devices, recovery through their own backups, shown once by copying the data folder to a fresh machine and opening it.
How much unsent work a lost device could cost is stated, and kept small by sending work as soon as there's a connection.
Migrations tried on data the size of production, made up where real data can't be copied.

overengineering.text: Tooling to restore a single tenant or record before anyone has needed it, when restoring to a copy and fixing by hand would do.
Backups and restore drills for output it can rebuild from a source that still has the data.
Backups and restore drills for software that keeps no data.
Downgrade migrations for every release of software that updates itself, where an older version can refuse newer data instead.

qualities.name: Efficiency
qualities.question: Is it fast enough, at a cost that makes sense?
qualities.why: It's fast enough for the work, at the load it gets, at a cost that makes sense.

implementation.text: Fast enough that those trying it can judge the idea.

overengineering.text: Optimizing, caching, load testing.
Caching a dependency's responses before its speed, cost, or limits get in the way of trying the idea.
Incremental loads or change capture, when a full pull of a sample answers the question.
Server-side rendering, code splitting, or a CDN for something a few people open.
Bundling into a single binary, or trimming startup time.

implementation.text: Fix what's slow enough to get in the way of real use.
Reads from systems others rely on kept light, such as off-hours, in pages, or from a replica.
Photos and large files resized before they're stored or sent.

overengineering.text: Load tests, caches, scaling work.
Incremental loads, parallel workers, or a distributed engine, when one process and a full reload finish in time.
A message queue or worker fleet, when a scheduled task handles today's volume.
Rate limits and quotas for each caller while only invited ones use it.
Memoizing, benchmarking, or bundle-size budgets before anyone has found it slow or large.

levels.summary: Fine at realistic volumes, with no runaway work.

outcomes.text: It works at realistic volumes.

implementation.text: Tried with realistic amounts of data and use.
Finishes well within its schedule at realistic volumes.
Starts quickly.
Long work, such as importing a large file, runs off the main thread with progress shown.
Tried on the oldest supported device and a slow connection, with a day's work captured offline and then synced.

overengineering.text: Performance targets, capacity planning.
Caches, read replicas, or a search engine before a real query is shown to be slow.
Incremental loads or change data capture when a full reload finishes well within its window.
Rewriting it, or bundling it into a native binary, to shave startup time nobody has noticed.
Delta updates, or shrinking the download, before its size is a problem.

outcomes.text: The work it does is bounded.

implementation.text: No query or call for each item in a list, and indexes where queries need them.
Paging, input size limits, and streaming instead of loading everything into memory.
Limits on what it accepts and returns are documented.
A cap on what it can send or spend, such as texts per hour, so a bug or abuse can't flood people or run up a bill.
Retries capped and spaced out, with work that keeps failing set aside instead of retried forever.
A limit on retries and concurrent deliveries to each receiver, so one slow one can't hold up the rest.
Reads from a source in pages or batches, within the rate limits it sets.

overengineering.text: Autoscaling workers ahead of a measured backlog.

levels.summary: Targets for speed and cost are set, and met with room to spare.

outcomes.text: It meets agreed speed targets at peak load, with headroom.

implementation.text: Measured targets for response time, throughput, or how long a job takes.
A load test at expected peak, with room to spare.
A run on the busiest day's volume, such as a seasonal peak, finishing with time to spare before its data is due.
Page load targets measured from real users' browsers, such as Core Web Vitals.
Benchmarks of the slow parts, on the devices or data sizes it's used with.
A startup-time budget for the common commands, checked in CI.

overengineering.text: Tighter targets than those agreed.
Real-user monitoring for a tool a known few people use on known machines.
Load tests of software that runs on one person's device.
Load tests of every endpoint, instead of the busiest and the critical ones.
Parallelizing or scaling out a run that already finishes well before its data is due.

outcomes.text: What it costs to run is known and acceptable.

implementation.text: What it costs per unit of work is known.
Fees charged per use by what it depends on, such as per message sent, counted in its cost, with an alert on unusual spend.
Memory, battery, and data use fit the devices it runs on.
The load it puts on the services it calls, such as calls per command and how often it polls, is known.

overengineering.text: Cutting costs beyond what's agreed to be acceptable.
Cost tracked per tenant or customer, when nobody bills or decides by it.
Tracking running costs for code that runs inside other teams' services.

outcomes.text: Its limits are known.

implementation.text: The rate limits and quotas of what it depends on fit peak use.
Alerts before it reaches a known capacity limit.
The largest tenant's or customer's data and traffic, not just the average, within what's been tested.
The largest amounts, precision, and input sizes it handles exactly, documented and tested at those limits.
Retries that back off with jitter, so many devices reconnecting at once don't swamp the service they call.

qualities.name: Security
qualities.question: Is it protected, and does it follow the rules?
qualities.why: Systems and data are kept safe as more people come to rely on it, and it follows the rules that apply to it.

levels.summary: Trying it out puts nothing real at risk.

outcomes.text: Secrets stay out of code, version control, and anything it ships.

implementation.text: Secrets in the environment, or a local file version control ignores, never in the code.
Providers' test keys or sandboxes while it's tried out.
Nothing secret built into what's shipped to people's devices or published, build-time settings included.
A key that has to ship in the app, such as a maps key, treated as public and restricted to the app and the APIs it calls.
A token read only from an environment variable or a prompt, never a command-line flag, so the tool stores nothing and it stays out of shell history.
Only the files meant to be published go into the package, such as with a files allowlist, so no `.env` or `.npmrc` ships.
Generated or scaffolded files refer to secrets by name, never contain their values.

overengineering.text: A secret store, scheduled rotation, or separate credentials for each environment, while it's tried out with test keys.
Keychain integration on every OS, when a file only the person can read keeps the token safe.

outcomes.text: It uses made-up data. Real data isn't copied into it, and isn't left open through it.

implementation.text: Sample data that's made up, not exported from production.
Made-up names, phone numbers, and email addresses that can't belong to anyone, such as `example.com` addresses.
Made-up files in the formats it reads, with the structure of a real one and none of its values.
When a real file or record shows a problem, a made-up one that reproduces it goes into the tests, never the real one.
Recorded responses from a real service scrubbed of real names, IDs, and tokens before they're committed.
Public reference data, such as published tax rates or postal codes, used as is. A client's own records aren't.
Real data kept out of notebooks, spreadsheets, chat, and local copies outside the systems approved for it.
Where it has to use a real credential or reach a real system, it runs locally, on a private preview, or behind a shared password, never on an open address.

overengineering.text: Sign-in, tenant separation, roles, or input validation for work that holds only made-up data and reaches no real system.
Dependency audits, license checks, or security reviews while it's tried out.

levels.summary: Real people and their data are safe with it.

outcomes.text: Only those allowed can reach real systems or data, and one tenant or account never sees or changes another's.

implementation.text: Every read and write scoped to the tenant or account making it.
A test, run on every change, that one tenant can't read or change another's records, even by guessing an ID.
Real data encrypted in transit, and at rest where it's stored, such as with HTTPS and a managed database's default encryption.
Sign-in on everything that reaches real data, with the tenant taken from the session on the server, never from what the browser sends.
Each API key tied to one caller, with the caller taken from the key, never from the request.
Webhooks and other messages carry only the receiving tenant's data, and go only to addresses that tenant registered.
Callbacks from providers, such as delivery receipts or payment events, checked as coming from that provider before they change real data.
Each person or pipeline uses credentials issued to it, never a shared or built-in one, sent only to the hosts they belong to.
The host a token is sent to comes from the tool's settings or a flag, never from a config file in a repo someone cloned.
With no sign-in of its own, data kept in the OS user's own profile, where only they can read it, on a device with disk encryption.
Where it has a sign-in of its own, data on the device belongs to the signed-in person, and work not yet sent is kept for them, not shown to the next person, when they sign out.
Its own read-only account on each system it only reads, made for the work and easy to revoke, and separate storage and output for each client it works for.
No state kept between calls that could carry one caller's data to another.
Published only by CI or named people, to the registry it's meant for, so it can't go public by mistake.
Where a client's system offers only a shared key, a test account until it issues credentials for each person or pipeline, before real data flows.
Copies it writes where others read them, such as warehouse tables, readable only by the people and roles allowed to see that data at its source.
A leaked API key stopped by disabling its record, until callers can rotate their own.
Separate credentials for each environment, with providers' test keys everywhere but production.
Each person's own token, kept in the OS keychain or a file only they can read, never in committed config, and redacted from debug output and errors.
Authorization headers, API keys, and tokens left out of request logs and error reports, for calls it receives and calls it makes.
API keys it issues stored hashed, and shown once.
Signing keys, store credentials, and publish tokens kept in CI's secret store, never in the repository or the project's `.npmrc`.
Established libraries for authentication and cryptography, never hand-rolled ones.

overengineering.text: Sign-in or tenant separation for work that holds only made-up data and reaches no real system.
Roles and permissions beyond what keeping real data apart needs, unless the client's rules call for them.
A separate database or deployment for each tenant, when scoping every query keeps them apart and no client requires more.
A sign-in of its own, or encrypting local data, on a device the OS account and disk encryption already protect, unless the client's rules call for it.
Certificate pinning, jailbreak or root detection, or app attestation, unless the client's rules call for them.
Key scopes, scheduled rotation, or self-serve key management before anyone relies on it.

outcomes.text: Untrusted input can't run as code or commands.

implementation.text: Parameterized queries, escaped output, and no shell commands built from input.
Data from other systems treated as untrusted, even the client's own, and escaped when put into emails, messages, or pages.
Addresses callers give it, such as webhook URLs, checked so they can't reach internal systems or cloud metadata.
Sort and filter parameters matched against a list of allowed fields, never pasted into a query.
No raw HTML rendered from input.
Config and rule files parsed as data, never evaluated as code.
Config read with a safe parser, with keys like `__proto__` ignored when merging.
Paths from config files and templates kept inside the repo, so they can't write anywhere else.
Commands a repo's own config names run like that repo's own scripts: shown first, with values passed as arguments, and without tokens they don't need.
Webhook addresses set by the team for each invited caller, instead of taken from requests, until callers can set their own.
XML read with external entities and DTDs turned off.
Cells that could run as formulas escaped in exported spreadsheets.
Anything that updates itself installs only updates signed by the publisher. Until then, builds are installed by hand.
In an Electron app, windows load only its own content, with context isolation on and Node.js integration off, and links open in the system browser.
Deep links, scanned codes, and notification payloads treated as data, and web views that don't give pages from the network access to native code.

overengineering.text: A self-update mechanism of its own, when a package manager installs and updates it.

outcomes.text: It depends on nothing less stable than itself.

implementation.text: Nothing it relies on is at an earlier stability level, such as a prototype service, or a third party's preview API.
A third party or client system with no stated level judged by what it promises, such as a preview label, a deprecation policy, or a support agreement.
A widely used package that stays at 0.x judged by how it's maintained and how it changes, not by its version number.
Endpoints or services still being built alongside it counted as early, and written down as a known gap until they settle.

levels.summary: Protected against misuse, and follows the rules that apply.

outcomes.text: It's protected against misuse at the level it's exposed.

implementation.text: Rate limits and input size limits.
Protection against cross-site request forgery.
Sign-in attempts limited, session cookies secure and HTTP-only, and sessions that expire.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 1.
The OWASP API Security Top 10 checked, such as object-level authorization and mass assignment.
What it receives is checked for who sent it, such as signed webhooks.
Webhooks it sends are signed.
API keys that can be rotated and revoked.
Only its own services can put work on its queue, and a message can trigger only what it's for.
Links sent in messages use unguessable tokens that expire, and open only what they're for.
A lost or stolen device can't be used to reach the data, through the platform's storage protection and sessions that can be revoked.
Windows reach the system only through a few named calls, such as an Electron preload script, each checking its arguments, under a content security policy.
Signed releases, so the platform or package manager can verify them.
Known vulnerabilities in dependencies found and fixed.

overengineering.text: A web application firewall, bot detection, or a bug bounty, before its exposure or a real incident calls for one.
OAuth, mutual TLS, or request signing for callers when keys over TLS are enough and nobody asks for more.
Encrypting local data with a key of its own, when disk encryption and the OS account already protect it and no duty asks for more.
Certificate pinning, jailbreak detection, or code obfuscation without a specific threat that calls for them.
Sessions so short that people have to sign in again while offline.
Rate limiting inside the tool, when the service it calls enforces its own limits.

outcomes.text: The legal and regulatory duties that apply to it are known and met.

implementation.text: Privacy duties met, such as exporting or deleting someone's personal data on request, with a deletion at the source reaching the copies it made.
Which duties apply confirmed with the client, such as whether its data counts as health records.
Rates and rules carry the dates they take effect, so a change in the law ships before it applies.
Rules about where data may be stored, and for how long.
Consent and opt-out for the messages it sends, such as honoring STOP replies, where the law requires them. Transactional messages, such as order confirmations, often don't need an opt-out.
An audit log where a law requires one, such as for health records.
Where data stays on people's devices, how long it's kept, and how it's deleted written down, so the client can meet its own duties.
The app stores' privacy details match what it collects.
The source of each rule it implements, such as a law or regulation, recorded next to the rule.

overengineering.text: A certification, such as SOC 2 or HITRUST, before a client or law requires one.
Column-level encryption or tokenized personal data that no duty or reader calls for.

outcomes.text: Personal data is collected only where it's needed.

implementation.text: Only the fields the work needs, with nothing kept just in case.
Functions and APIs take only what they need, such as a postal code instead of a whole customer record.
Personal data kept out of logs, error reports, crash reports, and analytics.
Error messages and debug output name what's wrong without repeating the personal data passed in.
Emails, texts, notifications, and webhooks carry no more personal data than they need.
Third-party services sent only what they need to do their part.
Copies it makes, such as reporting tables or exports, carry only the fields their readers need.
Location and other metadata removed from photos and files, unless the work needs them.
Device permissions, such as the camera or location, asked for only when a feature needs them.
The legal duties that come with it, such as consent, or an agreement with a provider that processes it, in place before the first real personal data arrives.

outcomes.text: Its dependencies are maintained, and licensed for how it's used.

implementation.text: Licenses checked when a dependency is added, against how it's distributed, such as copyleft code in an app-store app.
Dependency versions pinned, such as with a lock file.
A lock file published with it, such as `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, or a bundled build, so people install the versions that were tested.
A lock file for its own tests, with runtime dependencies as ranges so the software using it can resolve them, and as few of them as it can manage.
A supported Electron release, since older ones stop getting security fixes.

overengineering.text: Security reviews, compliance audits.
Rewriting a well-maintained dependency in-house just to have fewer dependencies.

levels.summary: Its sensitive parts are reviewed, and actions can be traced.

outcomes.text: Its handling of credentials, payments, personal data, and permissions is known to be sound.

implementation.text: A security review of sign-in and permission checks.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 2.
The checks in OWASP MASVS that fit its risk, such as for storage, network, and authentication.
A review of how it gets, stores, sends, and refreshes tokens, including what debug output shows.
A review of what its windows can ask the rest of the app to do, and of how updates are checked before they install.
A review of how API keys are issued, rotated, and revoked.
Data and logs kept no longer than they're needed, backups included.
Builds that can be traced to their source, with a list of what's in them, such as SLSA provenance and an SBOM, where others install or build on it.
Keys that sign releases kept in CI's secret store or a hardware module, usable by few people, with a plan for if one leaks.
A penetration test, where the risk warrants one.

overengineering.text: A penetration test or formal certification that neither the risk nor the client's duties call for.
Encrypting individual fields on top of encryption at rest, unless a duty or a specific risk calls for it.
Root and jailbreak detection, obfuscation, or anti-tampering beyond what the client's risk calls for.
Mutual TLS or signed requests from callers, when API keys over TLS meet the risk.

outcomes.text: Each part has only the access it needs.

implementation.text: Where a service offers no narrower token, a separate revocable token for each pipeline, with the missing scopes written down as a gap in that service.
Service accounts and tokens limited to what each part needs.
People's access to production limited to those who operate it, and removed when they leave.
The app's database user can't change the schema, and migrations run as a separate one.
Read-only access to the systems it reads from, and write access only to its own tables.
The narrowest token scope each command needs, and a deploy-only token in CI.
A publish token that can publish only this package, kept in CI.
Only the device permissions it uses.

outcomes.text: Sensitive actions can be traced to who did them.

implementation.text: The sensitive actions agreed, such as changing permissions, exporting data, or moving money.
An audit log of sensitive actions.
Staff reaching a client's data, such as for support, logged and visible to that client.
Who created, rotated, or revoked each API key, or changed a webhook address, recorded.
Manual reruns, backfills, and replayed messages recorded with who started them.
Who's acting, such as the person or the CI run, sent with each sensitive call, so the service's audit log records it.
Who published each version, and from which commit, recorded.

overengineering.text: Logging every action, instead of the sensitive ones.
A separate tamper-proof audit store, when the client's duties don't call for one.
An audit log of its own on people's devices or inside a library, when the service it calls or the software using it records who did what.

qualities.name: Compatibility
qualities.question: Does it fit with what's around it?
qualities.why: It works with the systems, platforms, and standards around it, and doesn't break those depending on it as it changes.

levels.summary: Kept apart, so it can't affect anything people rely on.

outcomes.text: It reaches only those who chose to try it, and from Alpha, the people the client has agreed it can reach.

implementation.text: Behind a feature flag that's off by default.
Opt-in for invited people or systems.
Turned on per tenant, only for the tenants who agreed to try it.
A separate environment, or a preview deploy.
A preview endpoint, or an experimental command or flag.
An experimental module.
A pre-release version on the registry it's meant for, such as under an npm `next` tag on the client's private registry.
A test build, through TestFlight or a Google Play testing track, not the public store listing.
A separate build or channel, not the public download or its auto-update.
Emails, messages, and other effects that reach people sent only to an allowlist or a sandbox, or logged without personal data instead of sent.
At Alpha, real messages sent only to people the client has agreed it can reach, such as a pilot client's customers.
A setting that stops sending to real people, for one tenant or everyone, without a release.
Where managed devices block unsigned apps, shown on the builder's machine or a VM the client approves.
Writes to a system others use go to its test environment or a test account.
Output written to its own tables or schema, and messages read from its own queue or subscription, never one something else relies on.

overengineering.text: Supporting several platforms.
A feature flag system for a new product nobody relies on yet.
A public store listing, screenshots, or preparing for public review while it reaches only testers.
Auto-update and signed installers for every platform while builds can be handed straight to the few people trying it.
Signing builds only to get past managed devices, while it can be shown another way.
Packaging for every install channel, when one is enough to try it.

outcomes.text: It's marked with its stability level wherever it's used.

implementation.text: The stability mark on what it adds.
The mark shown to those trying it, never in messages sent to their customers.
In a public store, the level shown inside the app rather than in its name, since stores may reject a listing marked beta.
Its level in the window title, About screen, or test build's notes, when the whole app is at that level.
Its level in the API reference and the OpenAPI description, or a preview path.
Its level in `--help` and the README, and a notice on stderr when an experimental command runs, so it doesn't break output scripts read.
A pre-release version until Beta, then a regular `0.x` release until GA, with `@experimental` or `@beta` on exports newer than the rest.
Its level in the docs or a comment on each table or file it writes.

outcomes.text: It can be removed without affecting anything people rely on.

implementation.text: Kept to its own code, data, and settings, so taking it out touches nothing else.
What it created in other systems, such as deployed services, records, or files in people's repos, listed or marked so it can be cleaned up.
Its own tables or columns, not changes to ones others read.
Reads from systems people rely on with a read-only account, in small batches or off-hours, and writes nothing back.
In an app people already have installed, behind a remote flag, with its data kept apart from what the rest of the app keeps.
Those trying it know where it keeps its data, and how to delete it.
New config keys optional, or in a section older versions ignore.
No new runtime dependencies, and no code that runs on import, in a package others already install.

overengineering.text: Compatibility promises, such as stable versions, or announcing changes.
Versioned URLs, paging, filtering, and a complete error format before those calling it have reacted to its shape.
A remote flag in a new app nobody relies on yet, when a test build already keeps it apart.
A version field or migrations for its config file.

levels.summary: Breaking changes are fine, as long as those trying it hear about them.

outcomes.text: Its interfaces follow the common standards for what it does, so others can work with it without surprises.

implementation.text: Standard formats, such as UTF-8 text and RFC 3339 timestamps with a time zone.
Standard codes, such as ISO 4217 for currencies, ISO 3166 for countries, and E.164 for phone numbers.
Methods and status codes as HTTP defines them (RFC 9110), and errors as problem details (RFC 9457).
Output on stdout, errors on stderr, meaningful exit codes, and the platform's usual flag style, with `--help` and `--version`.
Semantic HTML, with native controls before custom ones.
The platform's conventions for where data is kept, navigation, permissions, and sharing.
The language's packaging conventions, and semantic versioning.
Standard schedule syntax, such as cron expressions.
Email sent from a domain set up with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

overengineering.text: Testing on every platform.
Builds for operating systems, architectures, or module formats nobody trying it uses.

outcomes.text: Those trying it are told about breaking changes, which can still be made freely.

implementation.text: A message to those trying it, or a note in its changelog.
A message to those whose reports or queries read its tables, before a column is renamed or removed.
Each caller's technical contact known, so breaking changes reach whoever maintains the integration.
Those trying it in CI pin an exact version, so a breaking release reaches them only when they update.

overengineering.text: Deprecation windows.
Versioned paths, tables, or exports kept alongside the old ones before anyone depends on them staying the same.
Reading old config formats, or a command that migrates them.
A forced-update check, where expiring old test builds is enough.

levels.summary: Breaking changes are rare, and announced.

outcomes.text: It's available to everyone it's meant for, without opting in, on the platforms and environments it supports.

implementation.text: The project's normal release pipeline, with no opting in.
Released to some of those it's meant for first, where the client wants that, then to everyone, with no one needing to opt in.
Settings that differ between environments kept out of code.
Supported browsers listed.
Supported operating systems, runtime versions, and architectures listed.
Installs and upgrades cleanly on each supported platform.
The same version on every channel it's offered through, such as npm and Homebrew, released together.
Released through the channel its users get apps from, such as the public store, a business store, or the client's device management.
An installer the client's IT can deploy, such as an MSI or a signed package.
Writes to the tables its readers use, and sends to every real recipient.

overengineering.text: Supporting browsers, OS versions, devices, or runtimes nobody using it has.
Packages for every package manager before anyone asks for one.

outcomes.text: Those depending on it hear about changes.

implementation.text: Release notes or a changelog.
Those depending on it known, such as the teams or services that use it, so changes reach them directly.
What's new shown in the app after it updates.
A notice when a newer version is out, checked at most once a day and turned off in CI.

outcomes.text: Breaking changes are rare, and announced ahead of time where possible.

implementation.text: Versioning, so a breaking change is visible.
An OpenAPI description, checked on every change.
A deliberate change in results for the same input, such as a new rounding rule, released as breaking, even when no signature changed.
Messages and events checked against their schemas.
Files it reads keep being accepted, and exports others read change only by adding to them.
Tables others read checked against their schemas on every change, and changed by adding to them. A change in what a column means is breaking too.
Tests that pin `--json` output and exit codes.
Its public exports and types checked on every change, such as with an API report.
A warning when a flag, config key, or export that's going away is used, in a release before it's removed.

overengineering.text: Deprecation windows, compatibility guarantees.
Versioned copies of every output table kept side by side.
Running old and new versions of an endpoint side by side.
Reading every config format it has ever had, instead of a command that migrates old ones.
Versioning or documenting the local database's schema, when only the app reads it.

levels.summary: Stable: a breaking change is a new version, with time to move over.

outcomes.text: Its interface is stable: a breaking change comes as a new version, and the old one keeps working for a set time.

implementation.text: Semantic versioning, with deprecation warnings before removal.
A new version alongside the old one.
What counts as breaking written down for those integrating, such as that new fields and enum values may appear.
Deprecation and Sunset headers on what's being retired, with its use logged by caller so those still on it can be told.
Webhook and event payloads versioned and kept stable like the endpoints.
Its commands, flags, exit codes, `--json` output, environment variables, and config format all kept stable, with a deprecated flag still working and warning before it goes.
A deliberate change in results for the same input, such as a new rounding rule, treated as breaking, while a fix that makes results match the documented rules is a patch.
The previous major version still gets bug and security fixes until its deprecation window ends.
A changed table or file, or a changed meaning such as amounts that now exclude tax, comes as a new one alongside the old.
A reworked workflow offered alongside the old one, with exports, links, and integrations kept working, and pages people already have open still working after a release.
In software that updates itself, a reworked flow or format offered alongside the old one until the agreed date.
Exports marked `@experimental` or `@beta` are outside the semver promise, and the README says so.
Work already saved, such as a finished report or an exported file, opens and reads the same after an update.
Older installed versions keep working against the services they use.

overengineering.text: Keeping old versions working longer than the agreed window.
An old flow kept alongside a reworked one in an app only the client's staff use, when the client agrees a switch date and trains them.
A major version for every changed result, including bug fixes and rule changes everyone must adopt.
Keeping every old build working forever, instead of a minimum supported version raised with notice.
A new version of a table for a change that only adds to it.
Keeping human-readable output stable, when `--json` is offered for scripts.
Keeping the internal layout of its local data stable, when only the app reads it.
Treating a visual change as breaking, when no workflow, link, export, or integration changes.

outcomes.text: It's known to work on every platform it supports.

implementation.text: Upgrading from every supported version is tested.
Tests run on each supported platform and runtime version, installed through each channel it ships on.
For software it runs itself, tests on the one runtime it's deployed to, with the browsers or clients it supports listed.
The critical workflows run in each supported browser.
Installs and updates on the client's managed machines, such as without admin rights or through their proxy.

overengineering.text: Supporting or testing platforms nobody using it runs.
A test matrix of runtime versions for software that only ever runs on the one it's deployed to.
Testing on every device model, instead of the supported OS versions and the models its users carry.

qualities.name: Observability
qualities.question: When something goes wrong, does someone find out and see why?
qualities.why: When something goes wrong, someone finds out and can see why.

implementation.text: Console output is enough.
Outbound calls and messages printed to the console without credentials or personal data, so those watching can see they happened.
Counts of what each run read, skipped, and wrote, printed at the end.

overengineering.text: Logging setup, error tracking, metrics.
Product analytics, when watching people try it answers the question.
Crash reporting or analytics SDKs, which bring consent and privacy-label duties with them.
A logging dependency or debug hooks in the package.

levels.summary: Someone who looks can see what went wrong.

outcomes.text: When an error happens, someone looking can see what happened.

implementation.text: Error logs that include the operation, the IDs of what it was working on, and a request or run ID.
Logs that name the file, row, and step, not the values in it.
The tenant in every error log.
Each run logs when it started and finished, how many records it read, wrote, and skipped, and why it failed.
A request ID returned with every response.
The request ID from a failed call to a service shown in the error, so the service's owners can find it in their logs.
A `--debug` flag whose output, with secrets redacted, can be shared in a bug report.
Crash logs a developer can get at, and a way for someone trying it to send its recent log, with tokens and personal data left out.
Errors thrown name what failed and the input or config field that caused it, so the logs of the software using it show why.

overengineering.text: Dashboards, tracing, and alerts beyond what its host or scheduler sends for free.
Logging inside a library, when the errors it throws carry what's needed.
Sending logs from people's devices to a central service, when they can send a log with a bug report.
Data-quality frameworks, lineage tools, or freshness monitors.
Delivery dashboards or per-message tracking for outgoing notifications or webhooks.

levels.summary: Errors reach whoever runs it, without looking.

outcomes.text: Whoever runs it can tell it's healthy.

implementation.text: A health endpoint, with an uptime check.
How often key operations run and fail, and how long they take, is recorded.
A dashboard of its key metrics, such as traffic, errors, latency, and queue depth.
Row counts or totals checked against the source after each run.
A `doctor` or diagnostics command that checks its setup and connections.
A diagnostics screen showing what's waiting to sync and the last error.
Error rates for the calls it makes, from the logs of the service it calls.
Which versions are in use, and how many update downloads fail, from the update server's logs.
Usually not applicable: the software using it watches its own health.

overengineering.text: Service level objectives.
Metrics for every endpoint and caller, instead of the few that show whether it's healthy.
Usage telemetry from people's devices.
Tracing, or a metrics stack of its own, when the host's metrics and an error tracker show whether it's healthy.
Data lineage or data-quality tooling with checks on every column.

outcomes.text: Whoever runs it hears about errors, and failed or missed runs, without searching for them.

implementation.text: An error tracker that notifies people.
Failures that providers report back, such as undelivered texts or bounced emails, recorded and counted.
A notification when a run fails or doesn't happen.
Crash reporting, with consent.
Where crash reports can't be sent, a Send diagnostics action that saves redacted logs to attach to a bug report.
An unexpected error prints a short message and how to report it, with the version and redacted `--debug` output, instead of a bare stack trace.
Problems reach the issue tracker, with version details, and where to report one is stated in the package itself.

overengineering.text: Paging, distributed tracing.
A notification for every rejected record, instead of a count per run.

levels.summary: Problems are caught before users report them, with a plan for each.

outcomes.text: Whoever runs it finds out about failures that matter to its users before they're reported.

implementation.text: Automated alerts on error rate, latency, and availability against agreed targets.
Where the client runs the service, failed syncs sent as reports without the work's content, and failure rates by version shared by the client.
Where nothing may leave people's devices, each release goes to a few of the client's users first, with the update server's logs watched.
Whether its main workflows succeed is measured, not just whether it's up.
A scheduled check that runs a critical workflow in production, such as signing in to a test account.
Traces that follow a critical workflow across services, where it spans more than one.
Failures a provider reports back later, such as undelivered messages or bounces, watched and alerted on.
Alerts on lateness and backlog, not just failure, and checks on what each run wrote, such as row counts and totals against the source.
Crash and update-failure rates for each release, from reports people agreed to send, watched after every release.
Its version sent with every call, and failure rates by version from the service's logs, watched after each release.
Release candidates tried in the consuming services' tests before they're the default install.
A pre-release channel, so problems show up first with those who chose it.
A reminder well before signing certificates, developer accounts, and domains expire.
An agreed way to hear from whoever runs a service it depends on when that service has problems.

overengineering.text: Distributed tracing for a single service.
Alerts on every error or metric, so the ones that matter get lost.
Error budgets and burn-rate alerts, where alerts on the agreed targets catch the same failures.
Alerts on client errors, such as 4xx responses, that come from callers' own mistakes.
A data observability platform, when a few checks on counts, totals, and freshness catch what matters.
Telemetry from people's devices beyond the crash and failure reports they agreed to, or built into a library.

outcomes.text: Whoever runs it knows what to do about each failure.

implementation.text: Each alert links to a runbook.
Runbooks for deploying, rolling back, and diagnosing it.
A runbook for when something it depends on is down, covering what users see and how to catch up afterwards.
A plan for a suspected data leak: who decides, who's told, and by when.
A runbook for rerunning a failed run, backfilling a range, and replaying or discarding messages that were set aside.
A way to replay failed deliveries once the receiver is fixed.
A runbook for a bad release: stopping it spreading, publishing a fix through each channel, and telling those affected.
Runbooks for pausing a rollout, getting a fix through store review quickly, and recovering work from a device that won't sync.

overengineering.text: Runbooks for failures that haven't happened and aren't likely.

qualities.name: Maintainability
qualities.question: Is it easy to understand and change?
qualities.why: It's easy to understand and change, and easy to see what a change will affect, because its complexity is kept to what it needs.

implementation.text: Whatever answers the question fastest. Copying, hard-coding, and shortcuts are fine.

overengineering.text: Abstractions, configurability, cleanup, or structuring for reuse.
A deploy pipeline, containers, or infrastructure as code before anyone has decided to keep it.
A general rules engine, or a layer that hides which provider it calls, when the few cases being tried can be hard-coded.
A state management library, generated API client, or routing setup for a few screens of fake data.
A schema, validator, and version field for a config format only its authors write so far.

levels.summary: It follows the project's conventions.

outcomes.text: It's built the way the rest of the project is, so anyone who knows the project can follow it.

implementation.text: The language's linter, formatter, and type checker, run on every change.
The language's idioms, and the patterns the project already uses for similar work.
The project's existing architecture, with its layers, boundaries, and places things go, instead of a new one.
In a new project, the client's conventions or the framework's defaults, rather than a structure of its own.
Established libraries for solved problems, such as dates, parsing, and retries, instead of hand-rolled ones.
A README on setting it up and running it locally, and its configuration.
A README on running it by hand, for one date or one message.
Review by another engineer or an agent.

overengineering.text: Generalizing for cases nobody has asked for.
Interfaces, plugin points, or settings with a single use.
New layers, services, or architectural patterns it doesn't need yet.
A workflow orchestrator, when a scheduler and one script will do.
A plugin system for commands, or support for several config formats.
A config format that grows into a language, with conditions, expressions, or includes.
A general sync or offline layer for every kind of record, when only one or two kinds go offline.
Settings, theming, or branding for each tenant before a second client needs something different.

levels.summary: Its structure fits the shape it settled on, and shortcuts are cleaned up.

outcomes.text: Its structure matches the shape it settled on, with clear boundaries, so what a change affects is easy to see.

implementation.text: Boundaries and dependencies that follow its shape, such as domain logic that doesn't depend on its transport or storage.
Parts that can be tested on their own.
Business logic and sync in plain modules, tested without the UI framework.
Commands kept thin over the logic they call.
A note on how it's built, and the key decisions behind it.
Code and tests marked with the rules they implement and verify, so changing a rule shows what it touches.

overengineering.text: Ports and adapters, repositories, or an interface for every dependency, when each has one implementation and the domain is small.
Splitting it into several packages before anyone needs only part of it.

outcomes.text: Earlier shortcuts are removed or tracked.

implementation.text: Code that survived from the prototype or alpha refactored or replaced.
Shortcuts that remain recorded as known gaps.

outcomes.text: Every piece of complexity has a reason it needs now.

implementation.text: Real duplication combined once there's a second real use.

overengineering.text: Hardening or scaling for load it doesn't have.
Splitting it into separate services before one part has needs the others don't.
A workflow orchestrator, or pluggable sources and destinations for systems it doesn't connect to.
A plugin system for commands, when only the team adds them.
A rule engine or DSL, where plain functions and config cover the rules it has.

levels.summary: Anyone on the team can change it confidently.

outcomes.text: Another engineer can change it confidently without the author, and tell what a change will affect.

implementation.text: Names and structure that explain themselves, with comments only where the reason isn't obvious.
Dependencies between parts explicit, with no hidden coupling through shared state or globals.
Someone new to it can set it up and ship a small change from its docs alone.

outcomes.text: There's no dead code, untracked TODOs, or unexplained complexity.

implementation.text: Dead code, and flags left over from earlier levels, removed.

overengineering.text: Rewriting working code to a newer pattern just to make it look cleaner.

qualities.name: Supportability
qualities.question: Who's responsible, and where do people turn?
qualities.why: Someone is responsible for it, and those depending on it know where to turn and what to expect when it breaks.

implementation.text: Whoever is exploring the idea looks after it.
Feedback through the test track's own tools, or a message to whoever built it.

overengineering.text: Bug tracking, support.
An in-app feedback or bug-report form.

levels.summary: Someone owns it, and problems get written down.

outcomes.text: It has an owner who decides its direction.

implementation.text: A named person or team.

overengineering.text: Support commitments, on-call.

outcomes.text: Problems can be reported, and aren't lost.

implementation.text: Bugs recorded in the team's tracker.
Those trying it know where to report a problem.
Where to report a problem shown in `--help`, the README, the package's metadata, and with unexpected errors.
A Help menu item, or the test track's feedback tools, with the version filled in.

overengineering.text: A help desk or ticketing system for those trying it.

levels.summary: Known problems get fixed, and people can see them.

outcomes.text: Known problems are fixed as they're found.

implementation.text: Bugs triaged regularly.

overengineering.text: Support response times, on-call.

outcomes.text: Known problems are visible to those depending on it.

implementation.text: Known issues listed in the docs, the release notes, or its known gaps.

levels.summary: Long-term ownership, with clear ways to get help.

outcomes.text: The owner is responsible for it long term.

implementation.text: On-call, or someone to reach outside working hours, if it's critical enough.
Where failures outside working hours can wait, a check at the start of each day and a way to catch up, instead of on-call.
Reviews of serious incidents, so they're less likely to happen again.
Dependencies, runtime, and database kept on supported versions, and upgraded before their end of life.
Time planned for keeping up with each year's OS release and the stores' requirements, and for renewing signing certificates.
A support policy saying which versions get fixes, and for how long.

overengineering.text: Round-the-clock on-call for work nobody needs outside working hours.
Out-of-hours on-call for a nightly job whose output isn't read until morning, when a morning check and a rerun are enough.
On-call for a library, when its problems reach the team through its consumers during working hours.

outcomes.text: Those depending on it know where to get help, and what response to expect.

implementation.text: A support channel, with expected response times.
When it serves a client's own customers, which questions go to the client and which reach the team is clear.
A status page or announcement during an outage.
A notice to those who read its output when data is late or incomplete, and again when it's fixed.
A way to reach support from inside it, with the version and the diagnostics people choose to share.
A named contact at each team or system that integrates with it, so notices reach a person.

overengineering.text: A status page for software that keeps working when its services are down, or whose outages whoever runs those services announces.
A self-serve developer portal with sign-up and ticketing, for a handful of callers onboarded by hand.

outcomes.text: Someone other than the author can change and operate it.

implementation.text: More than one engineer able to work on it.
Where one engineer works alone, a handover note and shared access, so someone else could take over.
Building, signing, and publishing done by CI, with certificates, store accounts, and publish rights held by the client or team, not one person.
